questions.prompt: Put Waterfall's six phases, including the phase that almost always follows Release in a real project, in their correct sequential order.
items: Requirements (define what the system must do)
Maintenance (fix issues and support it for as long as it's live)
questions.explain: The simplified five-phase Waterfall diagram leaves out the phase that almost always follows Release in practice: Maintenance. The full chain runs Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, then Maintenance for as long as the system stays in use — usually the longest phase of all.

questions.prompt: A team is building a regulatory report with a legally defined format and a fixed delivery date, and the requirements aren't expected to change. Which delivery model does Lesson 1 say fits this kind of work, and why?
options: Waterfall, because it fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and well understood up front
Agile, because short cycles let the team adapt the report's format sprint by sprint
A hybrid approach, because regulatory work always requires a Scrum Master
Neither model applies, since reporting work isn't a software delivery problem
questions.explain: Lesson 1 gives a regulatory report with a legally defined format as exactly the kind of work Waterfall fits: stable, well-understood requirements up front, where the up-front planning and fixed phases aren't a cost, they're the right shape for work that genuinely isn't going to change underneath you.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the phase that almost always follows Release in a real Waterfall project — covering bug fixes and ongoing support for as long as the system stays in use — is called ________.
questions.explain: Maintenance is everything that happens after launch: bug fixes, minor enhancements, and ongoing support. It's easy to forget when a Waterfall plan is first pitched, but it's usually the longest phase of a system's entire life.

questions.prompt: Match each Scrum role to what it actually owns, per Lesson 2.
right: Facilitates Scrum ceremonies and removes blockers for the team
Everyone actually building, testing, and delivering the sprint's increment
The single person accountable for the backlog's priority order
questions.explain: The Product Owner is the single person accountable for the backlog's priority order. The Scrum Master doesn't manage the team's work — they facilitate ceremonies and clear blockers. The Developers are everyone actually building, testing, and delivering the increment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Scrum's actual promise is that at the end of every sprint, the team has produced a ________ — working software that could be released right now, even if the business chooses to hold it for a later launch.
questions.explain: A shippable increment, not just "finished feature" or "code that compiles," is Scrum's actual promise — "could ship today" is a higher bar than a ticket merely being marked Done.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a Scrum sprint's ceremonies and roles, per Lesson 2.
options: The Daily Scrum is the team synchronizing with itself on progress and blockers, not a status report to a manager
The Retrospective is where the team privately discusses what to improve next sprint
The Sprint Review is where the team demos the finished increment to stakeholders
The Scrum Master decides what gets built next and manages the team's day-to-day work
A story counts as done once a developer personally believes it's finished, even before its acceptance criteria are checked
questions.explain: The Daily Scrum is the team syncing with itself, not reporting to a manager. The Retrospective is the team's private discussion of what to improve. The Sprint Review is the stakeholder demo. Deciding what gets built next belongs to the Product Owner, not the Scrum Master. And a story isn't complete until its acceptance criteria are all met — a developer's personal sense of "done" isn't the bar.

questions.prompt: A developer marks their ticket 'Done' because the code compiles and passes a quick manual check on their own machine. Per Lesson 2's actual promise about a sprint's output, what's missing from that claim?
options: The work hasn't been shown to meet its acceptance criteria and reach a shippable increment — 'I think this is done' isn't the same as a checkable, releasable result
Nothing — once code compiles, the Scrum Master should mark the whole sprint complete
The ticket just needs a Daily Scrum mention before it can be closed
Nothing is missing, since Scrum doesn't require acceptance criteria for every story
questions.explain: A story isn't complete until its acceptance criteria are all met, and Scrum's real promise is a shippable increment — something that could be released right now. 'It compiles on my machine' answers neither of those; it's exactly the gap between 'I think this is done' and a shared, checkable definition of done.

questions.prompt: A card has sat in 'In Progress' three days longer than planned because its owner has simply been busy with other work — nothing outside their control is stopping it. Per Lesson 3, is this card 'Off Track' or 'Blocked', and why does the distinction matter?
options: Off Track — the work is simply taking longer than planned, which usually just needs more time or attention, unlike Blocked, which means a hard stop entirely outside the owner's control
Blocked — any delay beyond the planned time automatically counts as blocked
Off Track and Blocked mean the same thing in practice, so the label doesn't matter
Blocked — because the card has now been In Progress for multiple days
questions.explain: Off Track means the work is simply taking longer than planned — normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look. Blocked means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside the owner's control, like a pending approval or a broken test environment. Mislabeling a slow-but-unblocked card as Blocked points the team's help at the wrong problem.

questions.prompt: What is a WIP (work-in-progress) limit on a Kanban board?
options: A cap on how many cards can sit in one column at once, forcing the team to finish work before pulling in more
The maximum number of cards allowed on the entire board at any time, across every column
A deadline by which every card currently in a column must reach Done
The number of team members allowed to work on a single card at once
A limit on how many columns a Kanban board can have
The maximum number of sprints a single project is allowed to run
questions.explain: A WIP limit caps how many cards can sit in one specific column at a time. It forces the team to actually finish work before pulling in more, which is what moves cards all the way to Done — not just starts them, since a developer context-switching between five half-finished tasks is slower overall than finishing one before starting the next.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a board-wide cap, but a WIP limit applies per column, not to the whole board. The point is to stop one specific stage — like In Progress — from overloading with half-finished work, not to cap the total amount of work anywhere on the board.

questions.prompt: Match each real tool from Lesson 3 to how it's described there.
right: The most common board in software and data teams
Boards linked directly to issues and pull requests
Tightly integrated with Azure repos and pipelines
questions.explain: Jira is called out as the most common board in software and data teams. Azure DevOps Boards is tightly integrated with Azure repos and pipelines. Trello offers lightweight boards for smaller teams. GitHub Projects links boards directly to issues and pull requests.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a ticket's journey through the Dev stage, per Lesson 4, in the correct order.
items: Ticket Assigned — picked up from the sprint backlog
Branch Created — work happens isolated from the main codebase
Code Review — a teammate reviews the pull request
Merged to QA — automated and manual testing begins
UAT Sign-Off — the business confirms it meets the request
Deployed — released to production for real users
questions.explain: A ticket is assigned from the backlog, worked on an isolated branch, reviewed by a teammate before it merges, then moved to QA for testing, then to UAT for business sign-off, and finally deployed to production — code review happens inside the Dev stage, before QA ever sees the change.

questions.prompt: Match each environment in the Dev -> QA -> UAT -> Prod chain to the question it actually answers, per Lesson 4.
right: Is this safe and correct enough to bet the business on?
Is this what we actually wanted?
Does this work correctly, including cases the developer didn't think of?
questions.explain: Dev answers 'does this work at all?' QA answers 'does this work correctly, including cases the developer didn't think of?' UAT answers 'is this what we actually wanted?' Production answers 'is this safe and correct enough to bet the business on?' — and nothing reaches Production until every prior stage has passed.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about environment ownership in the Dev -> QA -> UAT -> Prod chain, per Lesson 4.
options: Code review happens inside the Dev stage, before QA ever sees the change
If the business rejects a change in UAT, that's a sign the requirements need another look, not necessarily a bug
Once something reaches Production, it's still only the original developer's problem to fix
QA is owned by a QA engineer or an automated test suite
UAT is owned by the developer who originally wrote the change
questions.explain: Code review sits inside Dev, before QA. A UAT rejection points at the requirements, not necessarily a bug. QA is owned by a QA engineer or automated suite. Once in Production, it's everyone's problem, not just the original developer's — and UAT is owned by the business stakeholder who requested the change, not the developer.

questions.prompt: A change passes every automated QA test, but the business stakeholder rejects it during UAT, saying it doesn't show the metric they actually need. What does this reveal, per Lesson 4?
options: QA and UAT answer different questions — code can be technically correct and still not be what the business actually asked for
The QA tests must have been run incorrectly, since passing QA should guarantee UAT approval
UAT is redundant once QA passes, so the rejection should be overridden
The change should skip UAT entirely next time and go straight to Production
questions.explain: QA answers 'does this work correctly?' while UAT answers a different question: 'is this what we actually wanted?' Code can clear every QA check and still fail UAT, because UAT is checking against the business's actual intent, not just technical correctness — which is exactly why one environment can't replace the other.

questions.prompt: Match each deployment strategy from Lesson 5 to how it reduces release risk.
right: Two identical environments, with traffic flipped between them instantly
The new version ships to a small slice of real users first
Instances are updated a few at a time rather than all at once
A toggle that ships code dark, then turns it on independently of deployment
questions.explain: Blue-green keeps two identical environments and flips traffic instantly, so rollback is just flipping back. Canary sends the new version to a small slice of users first. Rolling updates instances a few at a time. Feature flags ship code dark and switch it on independently of deployment.

questions.prompt: What does Continuous Integration (CI) actually automate in a CI/CD pipeline?
options: Every commit automatically triggers a build and a test run against the new code
Every change that passes is automatically promoted all the way to Production, with no further checks
A human manually triggers a build whenever they decide it's needed
The release checklist — approval, monitoring, and rollback planning — runs automatically
Another engineer automatically reviews and approves every pull request without human involvement
Feature flags are automatically switched on for every new deployment
questions.explain: CI means every commit automatically triggers a build and automated test run the moment code is pushed, without a human manually kicking that off — it's what catches 'I broke something elsewhere' before a human has to find it by hand.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Continuous Deployment, not CI. CI itself stops at build-and-test on every commit; automatically promoting a change all the way through to Production is the separate, further step that a full Continuous Deployment setup adds on top of CI.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a real release, per Lesson 5's release checklist and CI/CD.
options: A rollback plan is a known, tested way to undo a change if something goes wrong after deployment
Skipping release notes doesn't matter as long as the automated tests passed
Staging is a separate, production-like environment that sits between automated testing and the real thing
Continuous Deployment means a change that passes CI is automatically promoted all the way through to Production
Monitoring after a release only matters once something is already known to be broken
questions.explain: A rollback plan is a tested way to undo a bad release. Staging is a production-like environment between testing and the real thing. Continuous Deployment automatically promotes a CI-passing change to Production. Skipping release notes still costs someone later, and monitoring exists specifically to catch problems immediately after a change lands, not only after they're already known.

questions.prompt: Two days after the Regional Revenue dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it shows last month's numbers as zero for their region. Per the capstone's production-incident step, what should happen first?
options: Check the data pipeline and relevant environment to investigate the cause, and tell the regional manager you're aware of the issue and investigating it — not wait until it's already fixed
Immediately redeploy the dashboard to Production without investigating, since the fastest fix is always the right one
Wait until the issue is fully diagnosed and fixed before telling the regional manager anything
Tell the regional manager it's user error on their end and close the report without further investigation
questions.explain: The capstone's incident step asks what you'd investigate — which environment to check first and what to look at in the data pipeline — and what you'd communicate to the regional manager while still investigating, not after it's already fixed. Staying silent until a fix lands, or redeploying blind, skips the investigation and the communication both.

questions.prompt: Put these capstone deliverables, per Lesson 6's checklist, in the order the project actually walks through them.
items: Write user stories for the revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, and automatic-refresh requests
Build a Kanban board and move the top-priority story into To Do
Simulate Build & Test, including a QA test plan for at least one edge case
Simulate UAT and write a sign-off in the sales director's voice
Write release notes documenting what shipped and why
Handle a simulated production incident two days after launch
questions.explain: The capstone walks the sales director's request from user stories, onto a Kanban board, through simulated Build & Test, through a simulated UAT sign-off, into release notes, and finally a post-launch production incident — the same Dev -> QA -> UAT -> Prod shape from earlier lessons applied to one real request end to end.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a reasonable acceptance criterion for the automatic-refresh story is that the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by ________ each morning, with no manual steps.
questions.explain: Lesson 6 gives exactly this as a reasonable, checkable acceptance criterion: the dashboard reflects the prior day's closed sales by 7 AM each morning with no manual steps — specific and testable, unlike a vague 'updates automatically.'
